questions.question: What are the three fundamental drivers of cost with AWS?
questions.answer: The three fundamental cost drivers are compute (processing power), storage (holding data), and outbound data transfer (sending data to customers or the internet). Every AWS bill ultimately traces back to one or more of these categories, regardless of which specific services are being used.

questions.question: What is the difference between CapEx and OpEx, and how does AWS change this model?
questions.answer: CapEx (Capital Expenditure) is a large upfront investment in physical assets like servers and data centers — the traditional on-premises model. OpEx (Operational Expenditure) is pay-as-you-go spending for consumed services. AWS converts IT from a CapEx model to an OpEx model, meaning companies can stop paying for idle capacity and only pay for what they actually use.

questions.question: Explain the four main EC2 pricing models and when you would use each.
questions.answer: On-Demand is the default — pay by the hour with no commitment, best for unpredictable or short-term workloads. Reserved Instances offer up to 72% savings with a 1- or 3-year commitment, best for steady-state production workloads. Spot Instances use spare AWS capacity at up to 90% discount but can be interrupted — best for fault-tolerant batch jobs. Dedicated Hosts give you an entire physical server, required for certain software licenses tied to hardware fingerprints, and are the most expensive option.

questions.question: What is the AWS Pricing Calculator and when would you use it?
questions.answer: The AWS Pricing Calculator is a free web tool at calculator.aws that lets you estimate the cost of a proposed AWS architecture before deploying — no AWS account required. You would use it during the architecture design phase to compare pricing models (On-Demand vs. Reserved), compare costs across regions, and build a business case for a proposed infrastructure budget.

questions.question: What is AWS Trusted Advisor?
questions.answer: AWS Trusted Advisor is a free AWS service that continuously analyzes your existing account and provides recommendations across five categories: Cost Optimization, Security, Performance, Fault Tolerance, and Service Limits. For cost optimization, it flags things like underutilized EC2 instances, idle load balancers, unattached EBS volumes, and low Reserved Instance utilization. Basic checks are free for all AWS customers.

questions.question: What is AWS Cost Explorer and how does it differ from the Pricing Calculator?
questions.answer: AWS Cost Explorer is a free built-in Console tool that visualizes your actual historical and current spending, filterable by service, region, and account — it tells you what you've already spent. The Pricing Calculator, by contrast, estimates what you will spend before you build anything. They complement each other: use the Calculator when planning, use Cost Explorer to monitor actuals and identify trends.

questions.question: Name the six pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework.
questions.answer: The six pillars are: Operational Excellence (running and monitoring systems), Security (protecting data and systems), Reliability (ensuring systems work when needed), Performance Efficiency (using resources efficiently), Cost Optimization (spending at the lowest price for required value), and Sustainability (minimizing environmental impact). Cost Optimization is the fifth pillar.

questions.question: What is right-sizing in AWS, and why does it matter for cost?
questions.answer: Right-sizing is the practice of selecting the smallest instance type that meets actual workload requirements, based on real utilization data from CloudWatch rather than guessing or provisioning for theoretical peaks. It matters because AWS charges by the hour regardless of whether you're using an instance's full capacity — an m5.4xlarge running at 5% CPU is paying for 95% of compute capacity that delivers no value.

questions.question: What are S3 storage classes and why do they exist?
questions.answer: S3 storage classes are tiers with different cost and retrieval speed tradeoffs: Standard (instant access, highest cost), Standard-IA (lower cost, small retrieval fee), Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval (minutes to hours), and Glacier Deep Archive (lowest cost, hours retrieval). They exist because not all data is accessed equally — some is accessed constantly, some archived for compliance. Matching storage class to access pattern can reduce costs dramatically.

questions.question: What is an S3 Lifecycle Policy?
questions.answer: An S3 Lifecycle Policy is an automated rule that transitions objects between storage classes or deletes them based on age or access patterns. For example: move logs to Standard-IA after 30 days, move to Glacier after 90 days, delete after 7 years. This automates cost optimization so you don't have to manually move data, and ensures compliance with data retention requirements.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you identified and resolved a cost problem in a cloud environment.
questions.answer: (Situation) During a cost review, I noticed our AWS bill had increased 40% over the previous quarter without any new feature launches. (Task) I needed to identify the source and reduce spend without impacting production. (Action) I used Cost Explorer to filter by service and found SageMaker charges in a EU region were the primary driver — development instances had been left running after a proof-of-concept that was never cleaned up. I also ran Trusted Advisor which flagged several EC2 instances with under 5% CPU utilization over 30 days. I terminated the idle SageMaker instances and right-sized the underutilized EC2 instances. (Result) Monthly spend decreased by 35% in the following month, and I documented a cleanup procedure to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: A client says their AWS bill doubled this month but they didn't add any new services. Walk me through how you'd investigate.
questions.answer: (Situation) Unexplained billing increase with no new services launched. (Task) Identify the root cause quickly. (Action) I'd start with Cost Explorer, filtering by service and then by region to isolate which service drove the increase and where. I'd look at day-over-day trends to pinpoint when the spike started. Common causes include data transfer volumes spiking, a previously stopped resource being started again, a Lifecycle Policy that moved data to a higher-cost tier unexpectedly, or a new Auto Scaling policy that's adding more instances than intended. I'd then cross-reference with CloudWatch metrics for the flagged service to understand utilization patterns. (Result) Most billing mysteries are resolved within 30 minutes of systematic filtering in Cost Explorer.

questions.question: A startup asks you whether they should buy Reserved Instances on day one of their AWS deployment. What do you advise?
questions.answer: (Situation) New startup deploying on AWS for the first time. (Task) Advise on Reserved Instance strategy. (Action) I'd advise against buying Reserved Instances on day one. First, Reserved Instances lock you into a specific instance type, region, and sometimes AZ — if you right-size later (and you almost certainly will), you're locked into an inefficient configuration. The right approach is: launch with On-Demand, run for 3-6 months, use CloudWatch and Cost Explorer to understand actual usage patterns, and then buy Reserved Instances for the stable baseline you've identified. (Result) This approach ensures commitment matches actual need rather than guesswork, avoiding over-committed Reserved capacity.

questions.question: How would you design a cost-optimized compute layer for an e-commerce application that has 10x traffic spikes during holiday sales?
questions.answer: (Situation) E-commerce app with highly variable traffic — baseline year-round, massive spikes during holidays. (Task) Design a cost-optimized compute architecture. (Action) I'd use a layered pricing strategy: Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity that runs 24/7 year-round (locking in up to 72% savings on that base), On-Demand for additional capacity during moderate growth periods, and Spot Instances (if feasible) for batch processing and non-critical background tasks. The variable scaling would be managed by Auto Scaling Groups that respond to CloudWatch metrics. (Result) This mixed model captures maximum savings on predictable baseline while retaining flexibility and cost control during unpredictable peaks.

questions.question: Your team has 200 TB of application logs in S3 Standard storage. Logs older than 30 days are only accessed during quarterly audits, and logs older than 2 years are almost never accessed. How do you optimize the storage costs?
questions.answer: (Situation) 200 TB of logs with clear access pattern variation by age. (Task) Reduce S3 storage costs while maintaining access when needed. (Action) I'd implement S3 Lifecycle Policies: keep logs in Standard for the first 30 days (active access), transition to Standard-IA at 30 days (much cheaper, acceptable retrieval fee for quarterly audits), and transition to Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 2 years (very cheap, hours retrieval is acceptable for rare access). If there's a retention policy of, say, 7 years, add a deletion rule at that point. (Result) Moving the bulk of 200 TB to Glacier could reduce storage costs by 80-90% for that aged data, while still meeting access requirements.

questions.question: A developer on your team keeps forgetting to stop EC2 instances after testing, resulting in unexpected charges. What processes would you put in place?
questions.answer: (Situation) Recurring cost problem from forgotten development EC2 instances. (Task) Prevent recurrence without blocking developer productivity. (Action) I'd implement a combination of automation and monitoring: set up AWS Instance Scheduler to automatically stop dev instances outside business hours, create CloudWatch alarms that alert when EC2 spend exceeds a threshold, configure Trusted Advisor to run regular checks and notify the team, add tagging policies so all dev instances are tagged with owner and purpose (enabling cost allocation and identification), and conduct a brief team training on the cost impact. (Result) Automated stops eliminate the human memory dependency, while tagging and alerts catch anything that slips through.

questions.question: Explain the concept of 'matching capacity with demand' in AWS Cost Optimization. How is this different from traditional on-premises approaches?
questions.answer: (Situation) Fundamental architectural difference between cloud and on-premises. (Task) Explain the demand-matching concept and its cost implications. (Action) Traditional on-premises IT required provisioning hardware for peak demand — if you expected holiday traffic to be 10x normal, you bought enough servers to handle that peak, and those servers sat mostly idle the other 11 months of the year. AWS enables dynamic matching: Auto Scaling adds capacity when demand rises and removes it when demand falls, serverless services like Lambda scale to zero at zero cost, and you pay only for what's actively running. (Result) A well-designed AWS architecture might cost 60-70% less than the equivalent on-premises approach because you're not paying for idle capacity year-round.

questions.question: What is the shared responsibility model as it relates to cost optimization?
questions.answer: The AWS shared responsibility model for cost means AWS is responsible for the pricing of their infrastructure and services, and customers are responsible for how they consume and configure those services. AWS controls pricing structure, free tier offerings, and pricing discounts — but customers control which instance types they choose, whether they clean up unused resources, which storage tiers they use, and whether they implement auto-scaling. Cost waste almost always comes from the customer side: over-provisioning, forgotten resources, or choosing the wrong pricing model for a workload.

questions.question: How do Spot Instances work technically, and what application architectures benefit most from them?
questions.answer: Spot Instances use AWS's excess EC2 capacity — compute that isn't needed for On-Demand or Reserved customers. AWS offers this capacity at a steep discount (up to 90% off) but reserves the right to reclaim it with 2 minutes' notice when capacity is needed. Applications that benefit most share common traits: they can be checkpointed and resumed if interrupted (ML training with checkpointing, Spark jobs), they run in parallel so losing one node doesn't fail the whole job (distributed batch processing), or the work is not time-sensitive (overnight jobs, rendering pipelines). Real-time user-facing applications should not use Spot without very careful architecture.

questions.question: How would you build a business case for migrating from on-premises to AWS, focusing on cost?
questions.answer: (Situation) Company evaluating on-premises vs. AWS cloud migration. (Task) Build a cost-based business case. (Action) I'd structure the analysis around Total Cost of Ownership (TCO): on-premises costs include hardware purchase and refresh cycles (every 3-5 years), data center real estate, power and cooling, network infrastructure, IT staff for maintenance and patching, and idle capacity costs. Against this, I'd model AWS costs using the Pricing Calculator, using Reserved Instances for stable workloads and estimating dynamic scaling savings during off-peak periods. I'd include indirect savings from AWS managed services replacing manual operational work. (Result) TCO comparisons typically show 30-50% total cost reduction for variable workloads when accounting for all on-premises costs, not just compute unit prices.

questions.question: A company has 500 EC2 instances across 5 AWS regions. How would you approach a systematic cost optimization exercise for their entire fleet?
questions.answer: Start with discovery and data collection: pull Cost Explorer data for the last 3 months filtered by EC2, segment by region and instance type. Run Trusted Advisor across all accounts to get the underutilization flagging. Segment instances by workload type — production, development, batch, testing. For production instances, analyze CloudWatch CPU/memory/network metrics over 30+ days to identify right-sizing opportunities. For development instances, implement scheduled stops during off-hours (typically 65%+ idle time). For batch workloads, evaluate Spot Instance viability. Identify the largest Reserved Instance opportunities for the stable production baseline. Prioritize by potential savings — typically 20% of instances drive 80% of cost. Implement changes in waves, validating performance after each change. Target: 20-35% fleet cost reduction is achievable in most enterprises without performance impact.

questions.question: How does AWS pricing strategy differ from traditional software licensing models?
questions.answer: Traditional software licensing typically involves large upfront license fees, annual maintenance contracts (usually 20% of license cost), and per-seat or per-processor pricing that doesn't scale down when usage drops. AWS uses a consumption-based model: no upfront licenses, pay per second/hour/GB/request of actual usage, automatic price decreases as AWS achieves economies of scale (prices have been cut over 70 times since 2006). This shifts financial risk from the customer to AWS — AWS bets that as prices fall, usage grows enough to maintain revenue. For customers, the benefit is aligning cost to value: you only pay for what delivers business value, and costs decrease as the market matures.

questions.question: Explain how to design a multi-tier web application for cost optimization on AWS.
questions.answer: A cost-optimized multi-tier architecture would layer pricing strategies by tier. The presentation tier (web servers) benefits from Reserved Instances for the minimum baseline plus Auto Scaling with On-Demand for variable traffic. The application tier similarly uses Reserved for baseline plus Spot Instance capacity pools for burst handling (with proper interruption handling). The database tier uses Reserved RDS instances for production (steady state) and stopped instances for dev/test environments. For static assets, S3 with CloudFront eliminates EC2 web servers entirely for static content delivery. Data processing pipelines run on Spot Instances with checkpointing. S3 Lifecycle Policies tier stored data automatically. Cross-region architecture choices factor in regional pricing differences. The result is a system where each component uses the cheapest pricing model appropriate to its usage pattern.

questions.question: How do you balance cost optimization against reliability in AWS architecture?
questions.answer: Cost optimization and reliability have inherent tension: the cheapest option (single AZ, Spot Instances, minimal redundancy) is also the least reliable. The Well-Architected Framework addresses this by treating them as separate but equally important pillars. The key principle is that reliability requirements should drive architecture decisions first, and cost optimization should happen within those constraints — not at the expense of them. For example, a production database requires Multi-AZ RDS for reliability, but within that constraint you can still choose Reserved Instances over On-Demand. Spot Instances offer cost savings only for workloads that explicitly tolerate interruption by design — using them for production databases violates the reliability pillar regardless of cost benefit. The right question is always: 'What is the cheapest architecture that meets our reliability SLA?'

questions.question: AWS has cut prices over 70 times since 2006. What does this mean architecturally for how you approach pricing decisions?
questions.answer: This pricing history means a few important things for architects: First, specific pricing numbers should not be memorized or used in estimates beyond 6-12 months — use the Pricing Calculator with current prices, not historical numbers. Second, architectural decisions should be re-evaluated periodically; a decision made 2 years ago to use one service over another for cost reasons may have reversed as pricing changed. Third, new services often launch expensive and become significantly cheaper over time as AWS achieves scale — being an early adopter may mean overpaying initially. Fourth, and most importantly, the principles of cost optimization (right-sizing, matching pricing model to workload, eliminating waste) remain constant even as the specific numbers change. Design to principles, not to specific price points.
